chunks.text: 3 Dataset The dataset consisted primarily of H&E WSIs from toxicology studies conducted by Novartis Biomedical Research across global sites. The studies consisted of approximately 75% rodent (rat and mouse) and 25% non-rodent (dog, monkey, pig, and rabbit) species, ranging from acute (two weeks) to lifelong (two years) carcinogenicity studies. The training datasets were collected in two phases. In the first phase, 100,000 WSIs from rat studies conducted between 1999 and 2024 were obtained from existing internal digital databases. In the second phase, 1 million WSIs were acquired by digitizing archived glass slides from legacy rodent and non-rodent studies conducted from as early as 1967. We refer to the datasets as TOX-FM-100K and TOX-FM-1M , respectively. There was no overlap between the studies in the two training datasets. Overall, TOX-FM-100K was a less diverse dataset, consisting of WSIs from 700 rat studies only, while TOX-FM-1M was a more diverse dataset, consisting of WSIs from 13,352 studies across six species (rat, mouse, dog, monkey, pig, and rabbit). Additionally, TOX-FM-1M included more studies that were conducted at different contract research organizations, which introduced further variation in staining and scanning protocols, thereby increasing diversity. 3.1 Dataset Sampling and Curation Figure 2: (A) UMAP visualization of the hierarchical k-means clustering results at 4.0 mpp. Each point corresponds to one of the 100,000 bottom-level cluster centroids with the color indicating the corresponding top-level cluster centroid. Examples of the patches from the 16 largest top-level clusters are shown. Overall, the hierarchical k-means approach produces a morphologically coherent organization of the embedding space, with top-level clusters forming contiguous regions that correspond to visually distinct histological patterns.

(B) Examples of spatially linked patches selected by the progressive multi-scale strategy from the lowest magnification (4.0 mpp) to highest magnification (0.5 mpp). Patches (256 × 256 pixels) were sampled from the WSIs at multiple magnifications for training. For TOX-FM-100K , all non-overlapping patches from tissue regions were sampled at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 microns per pixel (mpp), resulting in approximately 1 billion patches. For TOX-FM-1M , a dataset curation method was implemented to sample a subset of patches, motivated by recent research on scaling dataset size for vision foundation models [ 10 , 22 ] , as well as practical considerations such as storage and computational constraints. The dataset curation resulted in a diverse and compact dataset of approximately 463 million patches, corresponding to approximately 4.4% of patches selected from a candidate pool of 10.5 billion patches across all magnifications. We used a progressive multi-scale strategy for sampling patches across the different magnifications, with selection proceeding from the lowest magnification (4.0 mpp) to the highest magnification (0.5 mpp). At the lowest magnification, all non-overlapping patches from tissue regions from all WSIs were defined as candidate patches for selection. Candidate patches at each subsequent higher magnification were restricted to those located within the regions of the selected patches at the preceding lower magnification. Figure 2 B shows examples of the spatially linked selected patches across magnifications. We used a hierarchical k-means approach [ 39 ] for the selection of patches, applying the method to candidate patches at each magnification. First, Midnight-12k [ 17 ] was used to generate embeddings for all candidate patches. The embeddings at each magnification were independently projected into a lower dimensional space using principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the computational cost of clustering.

Then, k-means clustering was applied to the embeddings and recursively applied to the resulting centroids, yielding a bottom-up four-level hierarchy of clusters. Given a target subset size, the quota was distributed top-down from the from the root clusters to the leaf clusters, where individual patches were finally selected. Specifically, at each level, the number of samples allocated to a parent cluster was uniformly distributed among its child clusters. If a child cluster had fewer samples than the allocated quota, the additional quota was reallocated to the remaining child clusters of the same parent. Figure 2 A shows the UMAP visualization of the hierarchical clustering results for the lowest magnification. Overall, the dataset curation strategy for TOX-FM-1M yielded spatially linked subsets of patches across magnifications. By balancing the selected patches across the hierarchical levels within a magnification, the method reduced the redundancy of common histological patterns, while preserving diverse and under-represented phenotypes. Across magnifications, rare tissue types were oversampled relative to the sampling ratio in most cases. More details of the settings used for the hierarchical k-means approach and a validation analysis of the method are provided in Appendix 1 . 3.1 Dataset Sampling and Curation Figure 2: (A) UMAP visualization of the hierarchical k-means clustering results at 4.0 mpp. Each point corresponds to one of the 100,000 bottom-level cluster centroids with the color indicating the corresponding top-level cluster centroid. More details of the settings used for the hierarchical k-means approach and a validation analysis of the method are provided in Appendix 1 . 5 Evaluation 5.1 Pathology Foundation Models We evaluated both non-clinical and clinical PFMs to assess domain-specific performance and cross-domain generalization. Table 1 shows an overview of the PFMs. Table 1: Overview of non-clinical and clinical PFMs for evaluation. The number of parameters for ViT-L, ViT-H, and ViT-g architectures are approximately 305M, 636M, and 1.1B parameters, respectively.

Domain Model Architecture Training Magnification (mpp) Non-Clinical TOX-FM-100K-ViT-L ViT-L 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H ViT-H 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H ViT-H 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL ViT-H 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 Clinical Prov-GigaPath ViT-g 0.5 H-optimus-0 ViT-g 0.5 Midnight-12k ViT-g 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 Non-Clinical Models. First, we developed TOX-FM-100K-ViT-L and TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H to evaluate the effects of scaling model size. While most state-of-the-art PFMs adopt ViT-g (1.1B parameters) architectures, we explored whether ViT-L and ViT-H architectures, which are approximately 30 – 60% of the size of ViT-g, remain competitive with significantly reduced computational costs. Second, we developed TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H to evaluate the effects of scaling dataset diversity and training with curated datasets, as well as to provide a baseline for the continual learning strategy. Finally, we developed TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL, which was initialized from TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H, to evaluate the continual learning strategy used to integrate knowledge from datasets collected in different phases. Additionally, we fine-tuned all models with the Gram anchoring objective on their respective training datasets and refer to the corresponding models with the -Gram suffix. Clinical Models. We evaluated state-of-the-art clinical PFMs with licenses that permit commercial use. Specifically, we evaluated Prov-GigaPath [ 12 ] , H-optimus-0 [ 13 ] , and Midnight-12k [ 17 ] , which were trained on various public and proprietary clinical datasets and have demonstrated strong performance across various clinical pathology benchmarks [ 46 , 47 , 48 ] . All models were accessed via the official versions published on Hugging Face. Natural Image Models. As baselines, we included out-of-domain models trained on non-pathology datasets.

Specifically, we evaluated a ViT-B (86M parameters) model trained on the ImageNet dataset of 1.2 million images [ 49 , 50 ] and the ViT-L variant (distilled from ViT-7B) of the original DINOv3 model trained on the LVD-1689M web-scale dataset of 1.689 billion images [ 22 ] . Although web-scale data may contain some biomedical or pathology-related images, such content is expected to represent only a small fraction of LVD-1689M, which is predominantly composed of natural images. Accordingly, ImageNet-ViT-B provides a lower bound baseline of a small natural image model, whereas DINOv3-LVD-1689M-ViT-L provides a strong baseline of an architecture-matched general vision foundation model. 5.2 Downstream Tasks We evaluated the PFMs outlined in Table 1 on a comprehensive set of 18 non-clinical and 9 clinical downstream tasks across various species, indications, tissues, and magnifications. The types of tasks included patch classification, slide classification, and segmentation. Table 2 shows an overview of the downstream tasks. 19,935 WSIs from 289 studies across all six species were used as an evaluation dataset to design downstream tasks for model evaluation. The evaluation dataset was completely independent and there was no overlap with the WSIs in the TOX-FM-100K and TOX-FM-1M training datasets. The WSIs were paired with either metadata containing species and tissue information or pathologists’ annotations for artifacts and lesions, which were used to obtain labels for the respective tasks. The pathologists’ annotations were constrained to a region of interest in the WSI and exhaustively annotated within the region using QuPath open-source software for digital pathology image analysis [ 51 ] . Annotated artifacts were related to slide quality issues caused during slide preparation or scanning, while annotated lesions were related to drug- or disease-induced pathological findings in the tissue. The non-clinical tasks were designed to encompass a range of task-appropriate magnifications. Species and tissue tasks were performed at lower magnifications, specifically at 4.0 and 2.0 mpp, respectively, as they are primarily associated with global semantic features of the image. Artifact and lesion tasks were performed at higher magnifications, specifically at 1.0 and 0.5 mpp, respectively, as they are primarily associated with local spatial features of the image. Figures 3 B and 3 C show some examples of the artifacts and lesions present in WSIs. Following the established best practices for assessing PFMs [ 11 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 46 ] , we designed all tasks as patch classification tasks using linear probe evaluation. For improved performance on artifact and lesion tasks, we also applied attention probe evaluation using attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) [ 52 ] to aggregate patch token embeddings for patch classification.

For improved performance on species and tissue tasks, we also designed slide classification tasks using ABMIL to aggregate embeddings across multiple patches sampled from a WSI. Finally, we designed artifact and lesion segmentation tasks using a simple U-Net decoder [ 53 ] . For each task, the relevant WSIs were split into training and testing datasets, and patches (256 × 256 pixels) were sampled accordingly from the WSIs. Classification tasks were designed to be balanced across classes. To enable fair comparison between models, we performed a hyperparameter sweep across different learning rates and weight decays where applicable. We report the performance from the best hyperparameter combination, which was determined by monitoring performance on a constant batch that was held out from the training dataset for the task. We report the macro F1 metric for classification tasks and the mean intersection-over-union (mIOU) metric for segmentation tasks. All PFMs were frozen for evaluation and only the respective probes were trained for the downstream tasks. All linear probe patch classification tasks and slide classification tasks used the concatenation of the CLS token and mean of the patch token embeddings of the ViT model. All attention probe patch classification tasks and segmentation tasks used the patch token embeddings of the ViT model. Clinical Downstream Tasks. We adopted the eva open-source foundation model evaluation framework for oncology [ 46 ] and included all accessible pathology datasets. We followed all evaluation protocols and metrics as defined in the official eva repository [ 54 ] . Note that the eva evaluation protocol specifies constant default hyperparameters. To enable fair comparison between models, we performed a hyperparameter sweep across different learning rates and weight decays where applicable. We report the performance from the best hyperparameter combination, similar to the evaluation protocol described for non-clinical tasks.

Overall, this improved performance by approximately 1 – 4% compared to the metrics reported on the official leaderboard for the clinical PFMs. More details of the hyperparameters are provided in Appendix 2 . 5.1 Pathology Foundation Models We evaluated both non-clinical and clinical PFMs to assess domain-specific performance and cross-domain generalization. More details of the performance on individual tasks are provided in Appendix 3 . Figure 3: (A) Distribution of task weights and overall performance (mean and standard deviation) of all models across a comprehensive set of 18 non-clinical and 9 clinical downstream tasks. (B) Examples of attention weights from attention probe evaluation for the artifact patch classification non-clinical task using embeddings from TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL. The attention weights were used to aggregate the patch token embeddings for patch classification. (C) Examples of segmentation masks for the lesion segmentation non-clinical task using embeddings from TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL.

Overall, domain-specific models achieve superior performance on their respective domain-specific tasks, with TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL demonstrating the best performance across the non-clinical PFMs and Midnight-12k demonstrating the best performance across the clinical PFMs. Notably, cross-domain performance remains remarkably competitive across both non-clinical and clinical PFMs. Specifically, the best cross-domain model achieves approximately 95% relative performance compared to the strongest domain-specific model and 98% relative performance compared to the weakest domain-specific model, suggesting effective cross-domain generalization. Figure 1 shows examples of the feature maps of Midnight-12k and TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL across different domains and scales using PCA visualization techniques, whereby the features are projected into 3 dimensions and visualized in RGB space [ 22 ] . Across both non-clinical and clinical images, TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL produces high-quality feature maps, capturing the semantic similarity of tissue morphology at different spatial locations across the images. Similarly, Midnight-12k also generates structured and informative feature maps, although some examples appear less spatially coherent by visual inspection. However, PCA feature map visualizations are qualitative and projection-dependent, so visual coherence is not necessarily a direct measure of downstream utility or predictive accuracy. We note that Midnight-12k was trained using the DINOv2 framework which uses learnable positional embeddings, which are interpolated to process images at varying resolutions. In contrast, TOX-FM models were trained using rotary positional embeddings [ 55 ] , which enables the models to process images at varying resolutions without requiring adaptation.

Therefore, while the PCA feature maps in Figure 1 are visualized at different resolutions to support qualitative analysis across multiple scales, additional examples of the PCA feature maps at the training resolution of 256 × 256 pixels are provided in Appendix 3 . Across the non-clinical tasks, we observe that the clinical PFMs tend to show the biggest gaps in performance on species and tissue tasks, which are performed at lower magnifications, while the performance remains more competitive on artifact and lesion tasks, which are performed at higher magnifications. Lower magnifications capture tissue-level architecture and organization, which exhibit greater differences between human and animal tissues, and may have lower transferability from the clinical to non-clinical domain. At higher magnifications, the distinctions between human and animal tissues are progressively reduced as cell-level details become the focus, resulting in stronger cross-domain transferability. We note that Prov-GigaPath and H-optimus-0 were trained exclusively on a single magnification at 0.5 mpp. While the underlying self-supervised learning frameworks [ 7 , 10 ] do implicitly learn multi-scale features through global and local cropping and scaling augmentations, the effective magnification range remains limited, and such augmentations alone are insufficient to capture the intrinsic multi-scale nature of WSIs. In contrast, models that explicitly include multi-scale datasets sampled at various magnifications such as Midnight-12k and TOX-FM models demonstrate measurably improved performance, particularly when evaluated across broader magnification ranges. While linear probe evaluation remains a strong baseline for assessing PFMs, attention probe evaluation significantly improves performance for spatially resolved patch classification tasks.

Specifically, using attention probe evaluation, Midnight-12k demonstrates a relative performance improvement of 18% and 10% on artifact and lesion tasks, respectively. TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL demonstrates an even larger relative performance improvement of 27% and 13%, respectively, suggesting that the patch token embeddings encode strong representations which can be appropriately leveraged using attention probe evaluation, but may be diminished when simply averaged for linear probe evaluation. Figure 3 B shows examples of the attention weights from attention probe evaluation using embeddings from TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL, whereby the relative importance of the patch token embeddings correlates well with the location of the artifacts. 6.2 Model Size Our experiments on scaling model size provide further insights into the performance characteristics of PFMs. First, scaling model size without dataset diversity appears to lead to overfitting and degraded cross-domain performance. Specifically, when scaling from TOX-FM-100K-ViT-L to TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H, we observe that overall performance improves on non-clinical tasks but decreases on clinical tasks. However, jointly scaling model size and dataset diversity, as in TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H, improves the overall performance across both sets of tasks. These observations also highlight the importance of broad and comprehensive evaluations for accurately characterizing the scope and limitations of PFMs. Without assessing the performance on clinical tasks, it may have been incorrectly assumed that scaling model size universally improves downstream performance, while the effects of overfitting would have remained unrecognized. We also found that the smaller model size of the non-clinical PFMs compared to the clinical PFMs does not appear to constrain performance on downstream tasks at this stage.

Specifically, despite TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL being 60% of the size of Midnight-12k, both models exhibit comparable cross-domain performance as detailed above. Alternatively, if model capacity was a bottleneck, we would expect non-clinical PFMs to perform substantially worse on clinical tasks than clinical PFMs do on non-clinical tasks, yet this asymmetry is not observed. 6.3 Dataset Diversity Our experiments on scaling dataset diversity demonstrate a difference in the impact on domain-specific and cross-domain downstream tasks. Specifically, scaling from TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H to TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H yielded more pronounced performance gains on clinical tasks than on non-clinical tasks. Motivated by observations from the natural image domain, we hypothesize that this is related to the difference in distributional proximity between the training and task datasets [ 56 ] . Under this assumption, TOX-FM-100K , despite being limited to rat studies, may already provide sufficient task-relevant diversity and effective representations for many of the non-clinical tasks, for which rat was the dominant species. Moreover, the pathologists’ annotations for artifacts and lesions were primarily performed on rat WSIs from recent studies, so the additional diversity across species, studies, and variation in staining and scanning protocols offered by TOX-FM-1M may be less relevant for these tasks. We performed a quantitative analysis to validate the assumption that TOX-FM-100K is distributionally closer to the non-clinical tasks than TOX-FM-1M . First, to make the analysis computationally tractable, random subsets of 100,000 patches were generated from each of TOX-FM-100K , TOX-FM-1M , the non-clinical task datasets, and the clinical task datasets. To ensure that each subset was representative of the complete dataset, subsets were stratified across magnifications, tasks, and classes where applicable.

Next, following the standard practice for measuring distances between data distributions [ 57 ] , we embedded each subset and calculated the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel [ 58 ] , sliced Wasserstein distance [ 59 ] , and Fréchet distance [ 60 ] between the training and task subsets in the embedding space. Figure 4 shows the pairwise distribution distances between the training and task datasets. To ensure that the results were not biased by the choice of embedding space, we repeated the analysis using embeddings from six models across the natural image, clinical, and non-clinical domains. Overall, the smallest distances across all metrics and embedding spaces are between TOX-FM-100K and the non-clinical tasks, consistent with our hypothesis. Additionally, the distances between the training datasets and clinical tasks are considerably larger than those of non-clinical tasks, supporting the view that the clinical tasks constitute a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark for non-clinical PFMs. UMAP visualizations of the datasets across all embedding spaces are provided in Appendix 4 . Figure 4: Average pairwise distribution distances (mean and standard deviation) between the training and task datasets across three metrics. Metrics are averaged across 5 random subsets of 100,000 patches from each dataset. Therefore, while previous work has emphasized the positive effect of distributional proximity and demonstrated the limited effect of dataset diversity on downstream tasks beyond the training distribution [ 56 ] , our findings suggest that both distributional proximity and dataset diversity may play different roles depending on the magnitude of the distribution shift. In the low-shift regime, distributional proximity remains the dominant factor for performance on downstream tasks.

However, in the high-shift regime, we observe that training with the more diverse non-clinical TOX-FM-1M improves the performance on clinical tasks, suggesting that dataset diversity can enhance cross-domain performance even when distributional proximity is absent. Motivated by recent work on the convergence of representations across models trained using different datasets, methods, and modalities [ 61 ] , we further examined whether scaling dataset diversity is associated with the convergence of non-clinical and clinical PFMs, thereby providing a potential explanation for the observed cross-domain generalization of TOX-FM models. Specifically, we measured the representation similarity of TOX-FM models with respect to Midnight-12k and H-optimus-0, the two best performing clinical PFMs on clinical tasks. We calculated the centered kernel alignment (CKA) [ 62 ] and mutual k-nearest neighbors (kNN) [ 61 ] metrics with null calibration [ 63 ] , which capture global and local representation similarity, respectively. The metrics were calculated using random, stratified subsets of 100,000 patches from the clinical task datasets. Figure 5 shows the representation similarity metrics between non-clinical and clinical PFMs. Overall, both global and local representation similarities increase alongside training dataset diversity, highlighting the increased representation convergence between non-clinical and clinical PFMs and consistent with the overall best cross-domain performance demonstrated by TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL. Figure 5: Average representation similarity metrics (mean and standard deviation) of TOX-FM models with respect to Midnight-12k and H-optimus-0. Metrics are averaged across 5 random subsets of 100,000 patches from the clinical task datasets. We observed very small variability for both metrics across the random subsets. We report the mutual kNN metric with k=100 but note that the same trend was observed for k=1 and k=10.

6.4 Continual Learning The continual pre-training strategy was found to be effective. Specifically, TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL outperformed both TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H (the initialization checkpoint) and TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H (the model trained from scratch) across downstream tasks, suggesting successful integration of knowledge from both datasets to yield the best overall performance among TOX-FM models. Figure 6 shows the performance trajectories on the non-clinical validation downstream tasks from the initialization through the selected checkpoints during training on TOX-FM-1M . By leveraging previous training efforts from the first phase on TOX-FM-100K , continual learning accelerated the convergence of TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL and fewer iterations were required to achieve peak performance in the second phase, reflecting the reduced incremental computational costs of updating models as new datasets become available. Figure 6: Overall performance (mean and standard deviation) trajectories of TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H and TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL on non-clinical validation downstream tasks during training on TOX-FM-1M . 6.5 Gram Anchoring Figure 7 shows the overall performance of TOX-FM models and the corresponding -Gram models on spatially resolved non-clinical and clinical downstream tasks. More details of the performance on individual tasks are provided in Appendix 5 . Overall, Gram anchoring demonstrated modest performance gains on spatially resolved downstream tasks, and benefits were more consistent across clinical tasks than non-clinical tasks. In particular, the comparison between TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL and TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL-Gram showed mixed results. For example, while Gram anchoring significantly improved performance on the artifact patch classification task using linear probe evaluation, the performance decreased using attention probe evaluation.

Similarly, Gram anchoring improved performance on clinical segmentation tasks, but the same effects were not consistently observed for non-clinical segmentation tasks. Figure 8 shows examples of the PCA feature maps of TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL and TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL-Gram. More examples are provided in Appendix 5 . The PCA feature maps are visualized at different magnifications and fields of view to compare the effects of Gram anchoring across different scales. Qualitatively, Gram anchoring feature maps seem to exhibit enhanced semantic coherence and reduced noise, especially at lower magnifications where spatial patterns of tissue structures are easier to discern visually. While the differences between the PCA feature maps are more difficult to perceive at higher magnifications, the impact on the performance of downstream tasks suggest that the effects of Gram anchoring persist across all scales. However, further investigations are needed to better understand the effects of Gram anchoring on the dense features and better identify the types of downstream tasks that may benefit from this approach, specifically for histopathology. Additionally, further exploration of techniques to improve the training procedure, such as checkpoint selection of the Gram teacher, may be informative as well. Figure 7: Overall performance (mean and standard deviation) of TOX-FM models and the corresponding -Gram models on spatially resolved non-clinical (artifact and lesion) and clinical (segmentation) downstream tasks. Figure 8: Examples of PCA feature maps across magnifications and concentric fields of view on an H&E WSI of femur tissue from a rat. The black boxes on each image indicate the field of view at the next higher magnification. 6.2 Model Size Our experiments on scaling model size provide further insights into the performance characteristics of PFMs. First, scaling model size without dataset diversity appears to lead to overfitting and degraded cross-domain performance.

Specifically, when scaling from TOX-FM-100K-ViT-L to TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H, we observe that overall performance improves on non-clinical tasks but decreases on clinical tasks. However, jointly scaling model size and dataset diversity, as in TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H, improves the overall performance across both sets of tasks. These observations also highlight the importance of broad and comprehensive evaluations for accurately characterizing the scope and limitations of PFMs. Without assessing the performance on clinical tasks, it may have been incorrectly assumed that scaling model size universally improves downstream performance, while the effects of overfitting would have remained unrecognized. We also found that the smaller model size of the non-clinical PFMs compared to the clinical PFMs does not appear to constrain performance on downstream tasks at this stage. Specifically, despite TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL being 60% of the size of Midnight-12k, both models exhibit comparable cross-domain performance as detailed above. Alternatively, if model capacity was a bottleneck, we would expect non-clinical PFMs to perform substantially worse on clinical tasks than clinical PFMs do on non-clinical tasks, yet this asymmetry is not observed. 6.3 Dataset Diversity Our experiments on scaling dataset diversity demonstrate a difference in the impact on domain-specific and cross-domain downstream tasks. Specifically, scaling from TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H to TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H yielded more pronounced performance gains on clinical tasks than on non-clinical tasks. Motivated by observations from the natural image domain, we hypothesize that this is related to the difference in distributional proximity between the training and task datasets [ 56 ] . Under this assumption, TOX-FM-100K , despite being limited to rat studies, may already provide sufficient task-relevant diversity and effective representations for many of the non-clinical tasks, for which rat was the dominant species.

Moreover, the pathologists’ annotations for artifacts and lesions were primarily performed on rat WSIs from recent studies, so the additional diversity across species, studies, and variation in staining and scanning protocols offered by TOX-FM-1M may be less relevant for these tasks. We performed a quantitative analysis to validate the assumption that TOX-FM-100K is distributionally closer to the non-clinical tasks than TOX-FM-1M . First, to make the analysis computationally tractable, random subsets of 100,000 patches were generated from each of TOX-FM-100K , TOX-FM-1M , the non-clinical task datasets, and the clinical task datasets. To ensure that each subset was representative of the complete dataset, subsets were stratified across magnifications, tasks, and classes where applicable. Next, following the standard practice for measuring distances between data distributions [ 57 ] , we embedded each subset and calculated the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel [ 58 ] , sliced Wasserstein distance [ 59 ] , and Fréchet distance [ 60 ] between the training and task subsets in the embedding space. Figure 4 shows the pairwise distribution distances between the training and task datasets. To ensure that the results were not biased by the choice of embedding space, we repeated the analysis using embeddings from six models across the natural image, clinical, and non-clinical domains. Overall, the smallest distances across all metrics and embedding spaces are between TOX-FM-100K and the non-clinical tasks, consistent with our hypothesis. Additionally, the distances between the training datasets and clinical tasks are considerably larger than those of non-clinical tasks, supporting the view that the clinical tasks constitute a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark for non-clinical PFMs. UMAP visualizations of the datasets across all embedding spaces are provided in Appendix 4 .

Therefore, while previous work has emphasized the positive effect of distributional proximity and demonstrated the limited effect of dataset diversity on downstream tasks beyond the training distribution [ 56 ] , our findings suggest that both distributional proximity and dataset diversity may play different roles depending on the magnitude of the distribution shift. In the low-shift regime, distributional proximity remains the dominant factor for performance on downstream tasks. However, in the high-shift regime, we observe that training with the more diverse non-clinical TOX-FM-1M improves the performance on clinical tasks, suggesting that dataset diversity can enhance cross-domain performance even when distributional proximity is absent. Motivated by recent work on the convergence of representations across models trained using different datasets, methods, and modalities [ 61 ] , we further examined whether scaling dataset diversity is associated with the convergence of non-clinical and clinical PFMs, thereby providing a potential explanation for the observed cross-domain generalization of TOX-FM models. Specifically, we measured the representation similarity of TOX-FM models with respect to Midnight-12k and H-optimus-0, the two best performing clinical PFMs on clinical tasks. We calculated the centered kernel alignment (CKA) [ 62 ] and mutual k-nearest neighbors (kNN) [ 61 ] metrics with null calibration [ 63 ] , which capture global and local representation similarity, respectively. The metrics were calculated using random, stratified subsets of 100,000 patches from the clinical task datasets. Figure 5 shows the representation similarity metrics between non-clinical and clinical PFMs.

Overall, both global and local representation similarities increase alongside training dataset diversity, highlighting the increased representation convergence between non-clinical and clinical PFMs and consistent with the overall best cross-domain performance demonstrated by TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL. We report the mutual kNN metric with k=100 but note that the same trend was observed for k=1 and k=10. 7 Discussion We present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained using the DINOv3 self-supervised learning framework on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets spanning a broad range of animal toxicology studies. We evaluate TOX-FM and state-of-the-art clinical PFMs on a comprehensive set of 18 non-clinical and 9 clinical downstream tasks, addressing key open questions regarding the role of domain-specific training and the capability of cross-domain generalization of PFMs between human and animal tissues. TOX-FM models showed the best performance on non-clinical downstream tasks, while clinical PFMs showed the best performance on clinical downstream tasks. This advantage of domain-specific training is further emphasized by the computational efficiency of the ViT-L and ViT-H TOX-FM models, which demonstrate superior performance on non-clinical tasks with only 30 – 60% of the model capacity of ViT-g clinical PFMs. While domain-specific models remain optimal, the cross-domain generalization capabilities of both non-clinical and clinical PFMs are notable, although transferability varies based on the type of tasks and the magnification at which the tasks are performed.

Further evaluation across both non-clinical and clinical domains, including broadening the scope and complexity of tasks across species, indications, tissues, and magnifications would be important to better understand where domain-specific models are necessary and where cross-domain models may be a viable alternative if domain-specific options are unavailable. We also highlight the importance of dataset diversity, which exhibited a stronger impact than model size, especially on cross-domain performance. To the best of our knowledge, we have provided the first analysis of cross-domain performance of PFMs across the non-clinical and clinical domains. The evidence of bidirectional cross-domain generalization observed in our evaluations suggests that PFMs learn domain-invariant representations that capture fundamental cellular or morphological features that are conserved across species. This could be particularly valuable in translational research, where a major challenge is the limited translatability of preclinical findings to clinical outcomes, resulting in many drug candidates failing to reach patients. By providing a potentially transferable representation space, non-clinical PFMs have the potential to bridge this gap and support the discovery and development of more robust predictors of clinical outcomes at earlier stages of the process. We also highlight the impact of distributional proximity and dataset diversity on downstream performance. In line with previous work [ 56 ] , we show that distributional proximity between the training and task datasets appears to be the dominant factor for performance on downstream tasks in the low-shift regime.

However, in contrast to previous work from the natural image domain [ 56 ] , we show that dataset diversity can improve cross-domain performance in the high-shift regime in the histopathology domain, as demonstrated by the strong performance of non-clinical PFMs trained on more diverse non-clinical datasets on clinical downstream tasks. TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL emerged as the overall best TOX-FM model, leveraging a continual pre-training strategy to effectively integrate knowledge from datasets collected at two different phases while maintaining efficient use of computational resources. We plan to use this scalable framework to continue incorporating new datasets as additional WSIs become available from future toxicology studies. More broadly, this highlights the value of continual learning approaches, which have become increasingly important amid the rapid growth of data and the expanding scale of foundation model development. Recent studies have proposed and evaluated a range of continual learning paradigms, focusing on the critical balance between plasticity and stability, as well as demonstrating the adaptability, efficiency, and sustainability of these methods [ 43 , 64 ] . We investigated Gram anchoring to improve dense feature representations for spatially resolved downstream tasks, including classification tasks focusing on artifacts and lesions, which may be very small, as well as segmentation tasks. Although we visually observed refinement of the dense feature representations with Gram anchoring, the impact on performance across the various non-clinical and clinical downstream tasks remains nuanced and task dependent. Additional analysis would be informative and help provide clarity on where Gram anchoring offers the greatest benefits in histopathology applications, specifically. Building on these advances, a promising next step is the development of PFMs trained on integrated non-clinical and clinical datasets.

By leveraging complementary information across domains, the current strengths of domain-specific models may be combined and support broader generalization. We plan to further investigate this direction in future work. One potential approach would be to curate harmonized datasets that include both non-clinical and clinical resources. For example, clinical datasets such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) [ 65 ] could be combined with TOX-FM datasets, with the dataset curation and sampling strategy applied to ensure balanced contributions across both domains. Alternatively, the continual learning approach could be extended across domains. For example, TOX-FM models could be continually pre-trained on TCGA, or clinical PFMs could be further adapted using TOX-FM datasets. While vision models continue to dominate the landscape of PFMs, multimodal foundation models developed by aligning histopathology with complementary modalities are emerging as a promising direction. Vision-language PFMs integrate histopathology with associated text from scientific textbooks, research articles, clinical reports, online educational platforms, and disease ontologies [ 66 , 67 , 68 , 69 , 70 ] . Vision-omics PFMs combine histopathology with matched gene expression profiles from sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics technologies, such as Visium and Xenium [ 71 , 72 ] . However, most development and validation efforts remain focused on clinical applications, especially oncology, and further investigations of multimodal PFMs focused on the non-clinical domain remain an important area of research. Notably, pathologists’ reports in toxicology studies contain descriptions of animal pathology findings, the Standard for Exchange of Non-clinical Data provides a framework for controlled terminology, and existing datasets pairing histopathology with spatial transcriptomics include samples from animal species, primarily mouse [ 73 , 74 ] .

Together, these resources may pave the way for more systematic development and validation of multimodal non-clinical PFMs, enabling the characterization of complex toxicity mechanisms across multiple biological scales and contexts. In this work, we address a critical gap in the development of foundation models for histopathology through the introduction of TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million WSIs consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. As PFMs continue to advance, rigorous understanding of the strengths and limitations of both non-clinical and clinical models is essential to fully leverage these tools to accelerate drug development and enable effective translation from preclinical to clinical stages and beyond. Towards this goal, TOX-FM establishes a benchmark for non-clinical PFMs while providing early insights into cross-domain generalization capabilities of existing clinical PFMs. Appendix Appendix 4: Dataset Diversity Figure A3 shows the UMAP visualizations of the two training datasets ( TOX-FM-100K and TOX-FM-1M ) and the two task datasets (non-clinical and clinical) in the embedding spaces of six models across the natural image (ImageNet-ViT-B, DINOv3-LVD-1689M-ViT-L), clinical (H-optimus-0, Midnight-12k), and non-clinical (TOX-FM-100K-ViT-H, TOX-FM-1M-ViT-H-CL) domains.
